newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FEATURE-Indonesian director soldiers on despite rejection.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Indonesian director soldiers on despite rejection.

text.p: He does well on the international movie scene. But at home in Indonesia, Garin Nugroho's films are constantly rejected by film distributors.
Instead of regular movie theatres, Nugroho's films are screened at university auditoriums or foreign cultural centres.

"Deep in my heart, there is an anger. But despite being angry, a creator has to keep creating things. A painter has to keep painting even though he does not sell anything," the 36-year-old Nugroho told Reuters in an interview.

Nugroho's movies blend art and sophisticated technique and are rich in improvisation. They also feature the ethnic richness of Indonesia's diverse cultures and the settings that take place in Indonesia's exotic settings.
Most viewers say they are impressed by the technique and details featured in his movies, but the plots can be hard to digest because of their complexity.
FILMS GRAB INTERNATIONAL AWARDS

Nugroho, clad in a dark purple shirt and grey jacket at his south Jakarta office, said his movies had been ignored by the national monopoly cinema chain owned by a relative of President Suharto on the grounds they were not popular.

"They think that my movies are not commercially popular, boring and so on. But they are invited by various universities for screening and discussions. There has not been any proof that my films are not popular," he said. Nugroho's "Bulan Tertusuk Ilalang" ("And the Moon Dances"), which tells of a love triangle involving two students and their teacher, won the top prize at Cambodia's first intern ational film festival in April. The movie, released in 1995, grabbed five awards at the International Berlin Festival, the Nantes Film Festival in France as well as the Singapore and Japan film festivals -- all in 1996.
Earlier in 1991, his "Cinta Dalam Sepotong Roti" ("Love on a Slice of Bread") won him a Citra, the local version of the Oscar, for best film and best director at the Indonesia Film Festival.
The year 1991 also marked the end of the festival because, organisers said, the Indonesian movie industry had stopped producing films good enough to participate in a festival.

"We have to make a difference between a commercial product and an art product. Like we differentiate between lovers of hand-crafted batik (decorated cloth) and those who only like the printed ones. I think there has been a wrong perception about my films," Nugroho said.

Nugroho's feature film "Surat Untuk Bidadari" (A Letter to an Angel") won him the Carridi D'Oro Award for best film at the 1994 Italian Film Festival in Taormina, Italy. His documentary on the island resort of Bali earned him a special award as the best tourism documentary at the Fotokino Film Festival in Cologne, Germany.
INDONESIA'S FILM INDUSTRY DYING
In line with the decline in the country's film industry, Indonesian cinemas are flooded with Hollywood and Hong Kong blockbusters.
Locally-made films available on the cinemas mostly feature soft-pornography while slapstick comedies are widespread on television screens.

A $1.24 million film "Fatahillah" which tells the story of a national hero who crushed a Portuguese attempt to establish a trading post in Java was launched last month in an attempt to revive interest in local films.
Indonesian movie observers, however, say the film was unlikely to resurrect the dying industry.

"The problem is the propaganda (of Fatahillah). A film should have the essence that is to entertain and not to serve as propaganda. If you want to make a thriller movie, please make a good thriller movie and so on," Nugroho said.
He said a market-oriented approach contributed to the decline in the movie industry in which professionalism, ethics and skills were neglected for the sake of the market.
TELEVISION SERIES ARE JUST 'EXHIBITIONS OF WEALTH'

Nugroho criticised the country's booming television industry. "Those television series are the exhibition of wealth of the newly rich people. It is an exhibition and not an entertainment. Nugroho has made some headway with Indonesian audiences with his 74-minute "Angin Rumput Savana" ("The Wind in the Savanna Grass"), which was aired in April at the TPI television network. The movie, jointly funded by John Hopkins University of the United States, the National Family Planning Board and the TPI, tells of friendship, love and revenge of people in the eastern island of Sumba.
When asked about his future, Nugroho said: "I am 36 years
old now and I have received many awards. I want to make better creation. I don't have the obsession to conquer those Hollywood movies...instead we have to learn from them."
